title: I Don’t Know Enough to Have an Opinion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author argues that one of a leader's most important choices is when not to offer an opinion. Beyond the obvious cases where a view would stifle discussion or bias a group, the higher standard is to withhold any opinion when you lack sufficient facts. Speaking prematurely can mislead the team and erode trust. Leaders who weigh in on everything dilute the credibility of the opinions that really matter. By contrast, a leader who is selective shows intellectual humility, and people take their stated views more seriously. The post ends by urging readers to make the phrase “I don’t know enough to have an opinion” part of their leadership vocabulary.
points: Leaders should hold back opinions when they would narrow debate or overshadow colleagues, but the higher bar is lacking enough information.
Premature opinions can mislead a team and damage trust.
Opining on everything lowers the weight of the opinions that deserve it, harming long-term credibility.
Admitting the limits of your knowledge signals intellectual humility and makes your later views more believable.
quotes: Sharing an opinion at the wrong time can narrow a discussion and discourage diverse viewpoints. Good leaders follow those ground rules before articulating how they see an issue.

They know speaking prematurely can mislead the team and undermine trust. So, they are cautious in any situation or on any topic where they don’t possess enough knowledge, facts, or data to offer a considered view.

Leaders who are quick to offer their opinion on nearly every topic harm their long-term credibility. Because they like the status of their authority, experience, and expertise, they enjoy putting their two cents into any discussion.

The intellectual humility they expose by limiting their opinions goes a long way in making themselves more believable. When they do articulate their views on matters where they possess insight, people take them more seriously.
How often do you use the phrase (or something like it): “I don’t know enough to have an opinion.” Make it a part of your leadership vocabulary. Others will respect you for it.
